transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I just haven’t been myself. I used to do things, you know—hiking, coaching, playing guitar. I was pretty active before. There was this trail I liked, out past the edge of town, and I used to know exactly where the light hit in the morning, but now I don’t even… I don’t go.

I don’t call people back much either. I’ll see the phone and know I should, and then it’s like I just sit there. In my rental—this small place—and hours go by. I’ll think, okay, get up, do the dishes, make a call, go outside, something… but I can’t seem to start. It’s not like me, and it’s been bothering me.
How long has it been since you started noticing this drop in motivation and interest in your usual activities?

It’s been… I guess about a year and two months now. It really started after I moved into that smaller rental, after the divorce. Things just kind of started unraveling from there. The place is too quiet, and the walls are this dull beige—reminds me of an office I used to work security in years ago, the kind with buzzing lights—and I don’t know, it’s like once I got in there, I stopped doing the things I used to do.

Over this past year and two months, has this low mood and loss of interest been present pretty much every day without a break, or have there been stretches—days or weeks—where you felt more like your old self?

There are some days that are… I don’t know, not as bad, maybe, but mostly I just don’t feel like myself anymore. It’s not like I suddenly wake up and I’m back to hiking or coaching or playing guitar like before.

I’ll be in that little rental, and I’ll know I should call someone back or clean up or just get moving, and I just sit there. Hours can go by. The phone will be right there, and I’ll think about it like it’s some big heavy thing. So… yeah, it’s been pretty constant, I guess. Not really stretches where I feel like the old me.
Over this same period, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual?

Sleep… I don’t know. I mean, I’m in bed sometimes, but that doesn’t always mean anything. The room has this heater that clicks on and off, and I’ll notice that more than I should, like I used to notice radio static on night shifts.

But whether it’s more or less than usual… I’m not really sure. I haven’t been keeping track. Some nights feel long, I guess, but I couldn’t tell you exactly.
During this past year, have you found yourself feeling unusually worthless, guilty, or overly critical of yourself?

I don’t know… “worthless” is a strong word. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, sure. Like when the laundry sits there or I don’t return a call, I’ll think, come on, just do it. But then I start thinking about other things, like how when I worked security there were these checklists and if you missed one little thing, the supervisor would circle it in red like it was a crime scene.

So… guilty? I’m not sure. Maybe not in that big way you mean. I mostly just feel stuck and annoyed with myself, I guess.
I’m sorry, I think I lost the thread there. What was the question again?

Before this past year and two months, have you ever gone through a similar period—maybe for a few weeks or months—where you felt this low or lost interest in things, and then came out of it and felt more like your usual self?

I’m not really sure. I mean, years kind of blur together for me. There were times I didn’t feel great, but I don’t know if it was the same thing or for a few weeks like you’re saying.

I remember after certain jobs ended, the days got kind of empty, but that could just be because the schedule was gone. When you work protective stuff, everything is times and rounds and doors and logs, and then suddenly there’s no log to fill out, so it’s hard to tell what’s mood and what’s just… no structure.

So, I don’t know. I can’t point to a clear period before this where I went down and then came back like normal.
Over this past year, have you noticed a significant drop in your energy level or feeling unusually tired most days, even without much physical exertion?

Yeah… I think so. It’s hard to separate “tired” from just not doing things, if that makes sense. Like I’m not out running around all day, so I shouldn’t be worn out, but I still just… don’t start.

I used to hike, and I coached some, played guitar, called people back. Now I’ll sit in that little rental place for hours, knowing there’s laundry or dishes or a phone call, and I just can’t get myself moving. It’s not like I climbed a mountain and need rest. I just don’t feel like myself anymore.

Sorry, I know you asked about energy. I guess the answer is yes, most days it feels like there’s not much there.
Over this past year, have you noticed trouble concentrating or making even simple decisions, like deciding what to do first when you have several small tasks?

I don’t know… maybe. I mean, everybody has trouble deciding sometimes, right? Like if there’s dishes and mail and the floor needs sweeping, I’ll look at it and sort of… stand there.

But then I start thinking about how I used to have checklists at work, and you just did the next thing on the log, no arguing with yourself. There was a radio, there were doors, there was a way to know if you were doing it right. At home it’s all loose, and I can get stuck in the loose parts.

So, concentration… I’m not sure how to measure that. I lose the point of things sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean.
Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight—eating noticeably more or less than usual, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

I don’t really know. I mean, I eat when there’s food there, mostly. Some days it’s just coffee and whatever’s easy, but I can’t tell if that’s appetite or just not wanting to deal with cooking.

Weight… I haven’t been tracking it. My clothes don’t seem wildly different, I don’t think. But then I’ve had the same belt for years, and those holes stretch out, you know? I remember at work people used to joke about gaining weight on night shifts because of vending machines, but that was more about routine than hunger.

So… I haven’t noticed a big change, I guess. Not one I could say for sure.
Over this past year, have you had any thoughts of death, dying, or that you'd be better off not being here?

I… I don’t know how to answer that cleanly.

I mean, people say things like “I’m dead tired” or “I wish I could disappear,” and sometimes that’s just talking. My dad used to say that after double shifts, like it was just a figure of speech, and nobody took it as… you know, something serious. I think about that sometimes, how people use those words and don’t always mean the same thing.

So if you mean, have I sat there making some kind of plan or something… I don’t think that’s what I’m saying. But the “not being here” part, I don’t know. Some days I just don’t want to have to keep showing up for everything. I’m not sure if that counts as what you’re asking.

Thinking back further, would you say this low, flat feeling and loss of interest has actually been going on in some form for two years or more, even before the divorce and move, or did it really start fairly clearly around 14 months ago?

I think it was more clear after the divorce, when I moved into that smaller rental. That was… about a year and two months ago, give or take.

Before that, I don’t know, I had bad stretches, but things still had structure. The old place had room for my tools and the garage shelves were labeled—funny what you miss, like knowing where the extension cords are. In the rental everything feels boxed up, like even the rooms don’t know what they’re for.

So two years or more… I wouldn’t say that exactly. It’s more like things started unraveling after I moved. Around 14 months ago sounds closer.

Would you say these feelings and changes have been severe enough to seriously interfere with your ability to work, maintain relationships, or handle daily responsibilities, or have they been more of a milder, nagging low mood that you've still been able to push through?

It’s… not mild. I mean, I tried to tell myself it was something I could just push through, like you do when you’re tired on a long shift, but it didn’t stay contained.

I got suspended from my protective service job after a routine patrol went bad. I scared some staff and people standing around, and after that it was like everybody looked at me different. I used to know that job inside and out—routes, doors, radios, all of it. Radios always have that one button nobody labels right, you know? But now I’m not there.

And since then I’ve kind of dropped out of everything else too. I stopped coaching, stopped volunteering, stopped answering people who used to rely on me. So, yeah… it’s been interfering. More than nagging.

Over these past 14 months, has this level of severity—where it’s really interfered with work and relationships—been constant the whole time, or have there been periods where the symptoms were less intense, even if you never felt completely back to normal?

It hasn’t felt like it ever really went back to normal. I mean, maybe some days I can get through the mail or make a phone call and it looks better from the outside, but the big parts… work, people depending on me… those stayed messed up.

After that patrol, when I scared the staff and the people standing there, and then got suspended, it was like a line got crossed. I keep thinking about the hallway lights in that building, how they buzzed even in the daytime—sorry, that’s not really what you asked. But since then I pulled away from coaching, volunteering, most of the people who used to count on me.

So, not constant every single hour, I guess. But severe enough the whole time that I haven’t really gotten my life back.
Have others noticed, or have you noticed yourself, that you're moving, speaking, or reacting more slowly than usual—or conversely, feeling unusually restless or fidgety—over these past 14 months?

Yeah… people noticed. I noticed it too, but more after, like looking back at it.

On patrol I’d start reacting before I could slow myself down. I remember crouching behind counters, signaling for people to get back, like there was no time to explain. And I kept repeating the last words people said to me, trying to check if it was part of… if it fit with what was happening.

There was this route I kept pacing over and over. Same hallway, same turn, same doors. The floor had those scuff marks near the vending machine—sorry, that’s not the point. Staff started looking scared of me, like I was the problem instead of helping.

So yes, not slow exactly. More restless, keyed up, reacting too fast.

Since that patrol incident where you scared the staff, do you find yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or vivid replays of that event popping into your mind, even when you don't want them to?

I don’t know if I’d call them flashbacks. That word makes it sound like a movie starting up, like you’re fully back there. I’m not sure it’s like that for me.

I do think about it, yeah, but then I think about all kinds of pieces from that place—the hallway, the way the counters were set up, how people were looking at me. Sometimes it’s hard to separate what’s a memory and what’s just me trying to sort out what happened.

So… unwanted memories, maybe? I’m not sure. It pops up, but I don’t know if it’s the kind of thing you mean.

Right now, are you still able to manage basic day-to-day things like feeding yourself, bathing, and keeping the rental reasonably livable, or has it gotten to the point where even those basic tasks are very hard to do most days?

I mean… I’m not completely falling apart like that. I eat something, eventually, and I do bathe, mostly. The rental isn’t great, but it’s not… I don’t know, it’s livable enough.

But I don’t feel like myself anymore. That’s the bigger thing. I used to hike, coach, play guitar, call people back—little normal things that made me feel connected. Now I’ll sit in that small rental for hours knowing there are dishes or laundry or a phone call I should make, and I just can’t get myself to start. It’s like I’m stuck before the first step.

doctor.question: Over this past year, have you noticed trouble concentrating or making even simple decisions, like deciding what to do first when you have several small tasks?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about trouble concentrating or making simple decisions, but the provided symptom profile does not include a cognition/concentration/indecisiveness item. The closest profile is negative symptoms, but its manifestation covers loss of motivation and social/activity withdrawal rather than concentration or decision-making.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… maybe. I mean, everybody has trouble deciding sometimes, right? Like if there’s dishes and mail and the floor needs sweeping, I’ll look at it and sort of… stand there.

But then I start thinking about how I used to have checklists at work, and you just did the next thing on the log, no arguing with yourself. There was a radio, there were doors, there was a way to know if you were doing it right. At home it’s all loose, and I can get stuck in the loose parts.

So, concentration… I’m not sure how to measure that. I lose the point of things sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

inference.note: Chronicity (~14 months, near-continuous low mood) with anhedonia, low energy, concentration difficulty supports persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) or a major depressive episode (F32.9) that has been unremitting; recurrent course unclear so F33.9 remains possible. No new features (psychosis, mania, guilt/worthlessness clearly endorsed) to rule out any candidate yet.

doctor.intent: Assess for another core MDE criterion (appetite/weight change) to determine if symptom severity meets threshold for major depressive episode versus milder persistent depressive disorder
doctor.question: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight—eating noticeably more or less than usual, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about appetite or weight changes, which are not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. I mean, I eat when there’s food there, mostly. Some days it’s just coffee and whatever’s easy, but I can’t tell if that’s appetite or just not wanting to deal with cooking.

Weight… I haven’t been tracking it. My clothes don’t seem wildly different, I don’t think. But then I’ve had the same belt for years, and those holes stretch out, you know? I remember at work people used to joke about gaining weight on night shifts because of vending machines, but that was more about routine than hunger.

So… I haven’t noticed a big change, I guess. Not one I could say for sure.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is a core criterion for major depressive episode and helps distinguish major depression from persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)
doctor.question: Over this past year, have you had any thoughts of death, dying, or that you'd be better off not being here?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of death or suicidal ideation, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know how to answer that cleanly.

I mean, people say things like “I’m dead tired” or “I wish I could disappear,” and sometimes that’s just talking. My dad used to say that after double shifts, like it was just a figure of speech, and nobody took it as… you know, something serious. I think about that sometimes, how people use those words and don’t always mean the same thing.

So if you mean, have I sat there making some kind of plan or something… I don’t think that’s what I’m saying. But the “not being here” part, I don’t know. Some days I just don’t want to have to keep showing up for everything. I’m not sure if that counts as what you’re asking.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this low mood/loss of interest has been present continuously for at least two years (supporting dysthymia) versus a more discrete ~14-month episode (supporting major depressive disorder)
doctor.question: Thinking back further, would you say this low, flat feeling and loss of interest has actually been going on in some form for two years or more, even before the divorce and move, or did it really start fairly clearly around 14 months ago?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: Things have been unraveling since I moved into the smaller rental after my divorce, about a year and two months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the low, flat feeling and loss of interest began, specifically whether it has lasted two years or started around 14 months ago.

patient.answer:
I think it was more clear after the divorce, when I moved into that smaller rental. That was… about a year and two months ago, give or take.

Before that, I don’t know, I had bad stretches, but things still had structure. The old place had room for my tools and the garage shelves were labeled—funny what you miss, like knowing where the extension cords are. In the rental everything feels boxed up, like even the rooms don’t know what they’re for.

So two years or more… I wouldn’t say that exactly. It’s more like things started unraveling after I moved. Around 14 months ago sounds closer.

inference.note: No clear evidence of a distinct prior depressive episode with full recovery, making recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9) less likely; symptoms have been persistent and fairly constant for 14 months with sufficient breadth (anhedonia, low energy, concentration issues, passive death thoughts), fitting either a single sustained major depressive episode (F32.9) or persistent depressive disorder (F34.1).

doctor.intent: Assess overall severity/functional impairment to determine if symptoms meet full threshold for a major depressive episode versus a milder, chronic low-grade pattern
doctor.question: Would you say these feelings and changes have been severe enough to seriously interfere with your ability to work, maintain relationships, or handle daily responsibilities, or have they been more of a milder, nagging low mood that you've still been able to push through?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I got suspended from protective service work after I scared staff and bystanders during a routine patrol, and since then I’ve pulled away from coaching, volunteering, and most of the people who used to count on me.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether the symptoms have seriously interfered with work, relationships, and daily responsibilities.

patient.answer:
It’s… not mild. I mean, I tried to tell myself it was something I could just push through, like you do when you’re tired on a long shift, but it didn’t stay contained.

I got suspended from my protective service job after a routine patrol went bad. I scared some staff and people standing around, and after that it was like everybody looked at me different. I used to know that job inside and out—routes, doors, radios, all of it. Radios always have that one button nobody labels right, you know? But now I’m not there.

And since then I’ve kind of dropped out of everything else too. I stopped coaching, stopped volunteering, stopped answering people who used to rely on me. So, yeah… it’s been interfering. More than nagging.

inference.note: Symptoms confirm persistent depressed mood, anergia, anhedonia, and functional impairment (job suspension) for 14 months without clear euthymic intervals, supporting a full depressive episode (F32.9) rather than just persistent mild dysthymia (F34.1); the incident triggering suspension and mention of scaring people raises possibility of more acute symptoms, but no clear psychotic or manic features reported. Keeping both codes as severity/chronicity distinction still unclear.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms have consistently met full severity (e.g., significant functional impairment, most symptoms present) continuously for the entire 14 months, or whether they have fluctuated in severity/number of symptoms below a major depressive threshold at times, to distinguish persistent depressive disorder from major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Over these past 14 months, has this level of severity—where it’s really interfered with work and relationships—been constant the whole time, or have there been periods where the symptoms were less intense, even if you never felt completely back to normal?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I got suspended from protective service work after I scared staff and bystanders during a routine patrol, and since then I’ve pulled away from coaching, volunteering, and most of the people who used to count on me.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly about whether the severity has interfered with work and relationships over the past 14 months.

patient.answer:
It hasn’t felt like it ever really went back to normal. I mean, maybe some days I can get through the mail or make a phone call and it looks better from the outside, but the big parts… work, people depending on me… those stayed messed up.

After that patrol, when I scared the staff and the people standing there, and then got suspended, it was like a line got crossed. I keep thinking about the hallway lights in that building, how they buzzed even in the daytime—sorry, that’s not really what you asked. But since then I pulled away from coaching, volunteering, most of the people who used to count on me.

So, not constant every single hour, I guess. But severe enough the whole time that I haven’t really gotten my life back.

inference.note: The severity of functional impairment (job suspension, loss of relationships, complete withdrawal from previously valued activities) for over a year without any period of normal functioning argues against a milder dysthymic disorder (F34.1) and instead supports a major depressive episode of moderate-severe intensity that has become chronic/unremitting. F34.1 is being deprioritized in favor of specifying severity within the MDD spectrum.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychomotor changes (retardation or agitation) to help gauge overall severity and distinguish moderate from unspecified depressive presentation
doctor.question: Have others noticed, or have you noticed yourself, that you're moving, speaking, or reacting more slowly than usual—or conversely, feeling unusually restless or fidgety—over these past 14 months?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down, like crouching behind counters, signaling people to get back, repeating their last words to check if they were part of it, and pacing the same route until staff looked scared of me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about changes in movement, speech, reactions, or restlessness/fidgetiness; this most closely matches the profile describing disturbed behavior and motor control, including reacting abruptly and pacing.

patient.answer:
Yeah… people noticed. I noticed it too, but more after, like looking back at it.

On patrol I’d start reacting before I could slow myself down. I remember crouching behind counters, signaling for people to get back, like there was no time to explain. And I kept repeating the last words people said to me, trying to check if it was part of… if it fit with what was happening.

There was this route I kept pacing over and over. Same hallway, same turn, same doors. The floor had those scuff marks near the vending machine—sorry, that’s not the point. Staff started looking scared of me, like I was the problem instead of helping.

So yes, not slow exactly. More restless, keyed up, reacting too fast.

inference.note: Added F32.2 given clear functional impairment (job suspension, loss of coaching/volunteering roles) suggesting severity beyond moderate; added F43.1 (PTSD) given the patrol incident with hypervigilance, repetitive pacing, echoing words, and reflexive defensive behaviors suggestive of a trauma response rather than purely depressive psychomotor change.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences intrusive memories, flashbacks, or distressing re-experiencing of the patrol incident, which would suggest a trauma-related process (PTSD) rather than depressive agitation alone
doctor.question: Since that patrol incident where you scared the staff, do you find yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or vivid replays of that event popping into your mind, even when you don't want them to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intrusive memories or flashbacks of a specific stressful event, which is not covered by the listed schizophrenia symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d call them flashbacks. That word makes it sound like a movie starting up, like you’re fully back there. I’m not sure it’s like that for me.

I do think about it, yeah, but then I think about all kinds of pieces from that place—the hallway, the way the counters were set up, how people were looking at me. Sometimes it’s hard to separate what’s a memory and what’s just me trying to sort out what happened.

So… unwanted memories, maybe? I’m not sure. It pops up, but I don’t know if it’s the kind of thing you mean.

inference.note: Patient explicitly denies classic flashbacks and reports only vague, mixed memories rather than intrusive re-experiencing, weakening support for PTSD (F43.1). Core depressive symptoms (anhedonia, low energy, psychomotor changes, functional impairment) remain prominent and persistent for 14 months, so distinguishing between moderate and severe depressive episode remains the focus.

doctor.intent: Assess the current degree of functional impairment (mild/moderate difficulty vs near-total inability to manage basic daily activities) to distinguish moderate from severe depressive episode
doctor.question: Right now, are you still able to manage basic day-to-day things like feeding yourself, bathing, and keeping the rental reasonably livable, or has it gotten to the point where even those basic tasks are very hard to do most days?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore—I stopped hiking, coaching, playing guitar, and calling people back, and some days I sit in that small rental for hours knowing there are things to do but I can't make myself start.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about ability to manage basic daily tasks and whether motivation/functioning has declined to the point that self-care and keeping the rental livable are difficult, which fits the negative symptoms profile.

patient.answer:
I mean… I’m not completely falling apart like that. I eat something, eventually, and I do bathe, mostly. The rental isn’t great, but it’s not… I don’t know, it’s livable enough.

But I don’t feel like myself anymore. That’s the bigger thing. I used to hike, coach, play guitar, call people back—little normal things that made me feel connected. Now I’ll sit in that small rental for hours knowing there are dishes or laundry or a phone call I should make, and I just can’t get myself to start. It’s like I’m stuck before the first step.

inference.note: Symptoms have been persistently severe for 14 months, causing marked impairment in work and relationships (job suspension, withdrawal from coaching/volunteering), with anhedonia, low energy, psychomotor agitation, and passive death-related thoughts—ruling out the milder F32.1 in favor of a single severe depressive episode without psychotic features.

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a persistent, non-fluctuating depressive syndrome lasting approximately 14 months, characterized by anhedonia, low energy, psychomotor agitation, difficulty concentrating, and passive thoughts of not wanting to be around, with clear functional impairment (job suspension, withdrawal from coaching/volunteering/social contacts). No prior distinct depressive episodes with clear intervening recovery were identified, arguing against recurrent depressive disorder (F33.2). No hallucinations, delusions, or other psychotic features were endorsed, ruling out a psychotic subtype. While trauma-related symptoms (hypervigilance, repetitive intrusive thoughts about the patrol incident) were explored, the patient did not endorse true flashbacks, avoidance, or a qualifying re-experiencing pattern sufficient for PTSD, making the mood disorder the primary and best-fitting diagnosis. The severity, breadth of symptoms, and marked functional impairment support classification as a severe single depressive episode without psychotic symptoms.
